topic: Compliance: SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, PCI, what FDEs actually do
why: In enterprise delivery the last mile is almost never engineering - it is a security review, a DPA redline, or a compliance lead asking where their data goes and who can read it, and an FDE who freezes there costs the deal weeks. You are not the auditor and not counsel, but you are the only person in the room who knows that the tenant isolation is Postgres RLS, that the classifier ships prompts to a third-party model provider, and that logs live in a SaaS for 30 days - and every one of those facts is a control someone has to sign. The skill is translating a customer's questionnaire into your architecture, answering truthfully with evidence, and knowing precisely where your authority ends and legal's begins.
prerequisites: Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems (topic 30): RLS policies, PII classification, envelope encryption and audit tables - the control map is a description of what you already built there, so if you cannot point at the policy you cannot claim the control.

Threat modelling and secrets lifecycle (topic 62): a data-flow diagram with trust boundaries and a secrets inventory, because a control map without a data-flow diagram is a guess about where the regulated data actually is.

IAM and cloud security (topic 15) plus Kubernetes security (topic 10): IAM roles, IRSA, no long-lived keys, KMS key policies, Pod Security and RBAC - these are the implementations you will cite as evidence, not aspirations.

Incident response and postmortems (topic 23): severity levels, an incident timeline and a comms path, because GDPR Art 33 (72 hours) and HIPAA breach notification (60 days) are incident-response requirements wearing legal clothes.

Observability (topic 21) and application security (topic 61): knowing exactly which fields end up in logs, traces and LLM spans, since the most common real-world compliance failure is regulated data leaking into telemetry.

The DefenderMate architecture in your head end to end: Next.js front end, webhook ingestion, Redis idempotency, Postgres with RLS, LLM classifier, HubSpot writes, S3 exports, weekly email - you cannot map controls onto a system you cannot draw from memory.

subtopics.name: Compliance triage: what the customer is actually asking
subtopics.learn: Learn to classify an inbound compliance ask into one of four buckets in under five minutes: (a) 'do you have a report' - send the SOC 2 / ISO cert under NDA, no engineering work; (b) 'does your architecture do X' - a factual question about your system that only you can answer; (c) 'will you contractually commit to X' - legal, never you; (d) 'we need you to build X before go-live' - a scoped engineering change with a date. Practise the sentence that buys time without lying: 'I can tell you exactly how it works today; whether we can commit to that contractually is a question for our counsel.' Write down the three facts you will be asked in every single review - where data is stored, who can access it, who else processes it - and have one-paragraph answers ready.

resource.label: Minimum Viable Secure Product (MVSP) - the baseline control checklist used in vendor security reviews

subtopics.name: SOC 2 anatomy: Trust Services Criteria, Type I vs Type II, scope
subtopics.learn: Know that SOC 2 is an AICPA attestation, not a certification, performed against the Trust Services Criteria: Security (the CC-series, CC1 control environment through CC9 risk mitigation) is mandatory, and Availability (A1), Confidentiality (C1), Processing Integrity (PI1) and Privacy (P1-P8) are optional categories the company chooses. Type I is design at a point in time; Type II tests operating effectiveness over a period, usually 3 to 12 months - so a Type I from last November is worth much less than a Type II covering the last twelve. Be able to say what 'in scope' means: which product, which environments, which subservice organisations are carved out versus inclusive. Understand the audit period gap and the bridge letter customers ask for when the report is six months stale.

subtopics.name: Reading a SOC 2 report properly, including the CUECs
subtopics.learn: Open a real report and navigate its five sections: the auditor's opinion, management's assertion, the system description, the test matrix (control, test performed, result), and unaudited other information. Go straight to two places most people skip - the exceptions column in section IV, and the Complementary User Entity Controls, which are the things the report says YOU must do (enforce MFA, review your users quarterly, configure encryption correctly). A qualified opinion or a page of exceptions is not automatically disqualifying; not knowing they are there is. Do this for your own dependencies: pull the SOC 2 or ISO certificate for AWS, your model provider and your log SaaS, and record for each what was carved out and which CUECs land on you.

resource.label: AWS Artifact User Guide - what it is and how to obtain vendor SOC, ISO and PCI reports

subtopics.name: The control map: the artifact and its schema
subtopics.learn: Build the spreadsheet a compliance lead will accept, one row per control, with these columns and no fewer: control ID; framework references (SOC 2 CC6.1, GDPR Art 32, HIPAA 164.312(a)(1), PCI Req 7); the requirement in one plain sentence; the implementation naming the actual mechanism (file, resource, policy name); the evidence artifact and how to pull it; the owner; the test frequency; and status (implemented / partial / gap / not applicable, with a written reason for every N/A). The two columns that separate a real map from theatre are implementation and evidence: 'access is restricted' is worthless, 'RLS policy tenant_isolation on 14 tables, enforced via SET LOCAL app.tenant_id in the request-scoped session; evidence = pg_policies dump plus the failing cross-tenant test in CI' is a control.

resource.label: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (NIST CSWP 29) - Organizational Profiles and informative-reference mappings

subtopics.name: Evidence that survives an auditor: populations, completeness, sampling
subtopics.learn: Auditors do not want a screenshot, they want a complete population and a sample from it. For 'every production change was reviewed', the population is every merge to main in the period; you must be able to produce it (GitHub API or CI records), prove the list is complete, and then show the approver on a sample. Learn the three evidence grades: continuous machine-generated (AWS Config rule evaluations, Security Hub findings, CI job results), point-in-time exports (IAM credential report, pg_policies dump), and screenshots (weakest, undated, contested). Build one evidence collector now - a script that writes dated JSON per control into an evidence/ directory - so evidence is a byproduct of the system rather than a two-week scramble in the week before the audit.

subtopics.name: Change management and access review as evidence-producing controls
subtopics.learn: Two control families come up in every SOC 2 and every questionnaire, and both are cheap to make auditable. Change management: protected main branch, required reviews with CODEOWNERS, required status checks, linear history, and a documented emergency-change path that still creates a record after the fact - the failure is not lacking a process, it is having an undocumented break-glass. Access: joiner-mover-leaver driven by IdP groups rather than manual grants, MFA enforced, no long-lived cloud keys (IRSA / OIDC federation from CI), and a quarterly access review whose output is a dated artifact listing every human and machine principal with prod access and the reviewer's decision. Pull the IAM credential report and the repo's collaborator list today and see how many stale principals you find.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - configuring branches and merges (protection rules)

subtopics.name: Encryption and key management claims you can actually defend
subtopics.learn: 'Encrypted at rest' is the most over-claimed control in enterprise software. Know precisely what RDS/EBS/S3 default encryption buys (protection against physical media and snapshot exfiltration) and what it does not (anything about which application, engineer or query can read the plaintext). Learn the vocabulary you will be asked about: envelope encryption, CMK versus AWS-managed key, key policy versus IAM policy, kms:Decrypt against kms:GenerateDataKey, automatic key rotation, and BYOK/HYOK when a customer demands to hold the key. Understand crypto-shredding - a per-tenant data key whose deletion renders that tenant's data unrecoverable - because it is often the only workable answer to erasure inside immutable backups. For transit, be able to state the TLS version and where termination happens, including in-cluster hops.

resource.label: AWS KMS Developer Guide - concepts and key policies

subtopics.name: Audit trails, log retention and the telemetry leak
subtopics.learn: Three distinct audit layers get conflated: infrastructure (CloudTrail organisation trail with log file validation and digest files, plus the Kubernetes API audit policy), database (pgaudit or logical audit tables), and application (who did what to which tenant's record, immutable, append-only). Decide retention deliberately per layer - one year is the common SOC 2 expectation, HIPAA documentation retention is six years, GDPR storage limitation pushes the other way - and write the number down. Then do the thing that actually matters: grep your logging, tracing and LLM-observability payloads for regulated fields. Prompts, completions, span attributes and error payloads carrying names, emails, PHI or full request bodies into a third-party log SaaS is the single most common real-world violation.

resource.label: AWS CloudTrail User Guide (trails, validation, retention)

subtopics.name: GDPR core: controller vs processor, lawful basis, Art 28 and subprocessors
subtopics.learn: Get the role right first, because everything follows from it: your customer is normally the controller and you are the processor acting on documented instructions, but the moment you use their data to improve your own product you have become a controller and inherited a lawful-basis problem. Know Art 6(1)(a)-(f) well enough to recognise that B2B SaaS usually rests on contract or legitimate interests, and that Art 9 special-category data (health, biometrics) needs a separate condition. Read Art 28(3) and be able to list what the DPA must contain - documented instructions, confidentiality, Art 32 security, subprocessor terms, assistance with data-subject rights and breach notification, deletion or return at end of contract, audit rights. Then produce your subprocessor list: cloud region, model provider, log SaaS, email sender, CRM - and know the notice-and-objection mechanics for adding one.

resource.label: EDPB Guidelines 07/2020 on the concepts of controller and processor in the GDPR

subtopics.name: RoPA, DSARs and erasure across a real stack
subtopics.learn: Write the Art 30 record of processing for DefenderMate - purposes, categories of data subjects and data, recipients, transfers, retention, security measures - and use it as the inventory that drives everything else. Then design the Art 17 erasure path and confront every store: Postgres rows (and referencing tables, and soft-deleted rows), Redis idempotency keys, S3 exports (versioned buckets need version deletes plus noncurrent-version lifecycle), the search or vector index, Kafka topics (tombstones plus compaction, not deletes), the warehouse, application and third-party logs, the LLM provider's retention window, and downstream systems like HubSpot. Backups are the honest hard case: the accepted answer is a documented rolling retention window plus a rule that restored data is re-processed for deletion, or crypto-shredding - not a claim you surgically edited a snapshot. Also know Art 15 access, Art 20 portability and the one-month response clock.

resource.label: ICO guidance - Right to erasure, including how it applies to backups and third parties

subtopics.name: Art 32 security, the 72-hour breach clock, DPIAs and transfers
subtopics.learn: Art 32 names four things auditors quote back at you: pseudonymisation and encryption, ongoing confidentiality/integrity/availability/resilience, restoration after an incident, and regular testing of measures - so your DR test and your pentest are compliance evidence, not just engineering hygiene. Art 33 gives the controller 72 hours from becoming aware to notify the supervisory authority, which means your job as processor is to notify the customer 'without undue delay' and to be able to answer, fast: what categories of data, how many subjects, what window, what was accessed versus merely exposed. Rehearse that you cannot answer any of it without the audit trail from the previous subtopic. Know when a DPIA is triggered (Art 35: systematic large-scale monitoring, special-category data at scale, automated decisions with legal effect) and the transfer rules in Chapter V: adequacy, SCCs plus a transfer impact assessment, and what a data-residency demand actually costs you architecturally.

resource.label: EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 on personal data breach notification under GDPR

subtopics.name: HIPAA vocabulary and the BAA boundary
subtopics.learn: Learn the terms precisely because misusing them destroys credibility instantly: PHI and ePHI, covered entity versus business associate (you are almost always a BA, and your model provider and log SaaS become subcontractor BAs), and the Business Associate Agreement that must exist before a single record flows. Know the Security Rule structure at 45 CFR 164.308/310/312 - administrative, physical, technical safeguards - and the required-versus-addressable distinction at 164.306(d): addressable does not mean optional, it means implement it or document why an equivalent measure is reasonable. Memorise the technical safeguards list (access control with unique user identification and emergency access, audit controls, integrity, person or entity authentication, transmission security) and the minimum-necessary principle. Know that breach notification runs to 60 days with a 500-record threshold that changes who gets told when, and that 'HIPAA compliant' is never a property of a cloud service, only of how you configure an eligible service under a BAA.

subtopics.name: De-identification: Safe Harbor vs Expert Determination
subtopics.learn: The highest-leverage move in a healthcare engagement is getting the data out of scope. Learn the two lawful routes at 164.514(b): Safe Harbor, which removes 18 enumerated identifiers (names, all geographic subdivisions smaller than a state, all date elements finer than year, ages over 89, phone, email, MRN, device identifiers, full-face photos, any other unique identifying number) with no actual knowledge of residual re-identification risk; and Expert Determination, where a qualified statistician certifies very small risk, which is what you need if you must keep dates or fine-grained geography. Understand that a limited data set under a data use agreement is a third, middle option. Then apply it: decide whether the LLM classifier can operate on de-identified text, and whether tokenising identifiers before the prompt moves the model provider out of BA scope entirely.

resource.label: HHS - Guidance on De-identification of PHI

subtopics.name: PCI DSS: scope reduction is the whole game
subtopics.learn: Learn just enough vocabulary to be useful and dangerous in the right direction: the cardholder data environment, PAN, sensitive authentication data (full track data, CVV2, PIN - never storable after authorisation, even encrypted), truncation and tokenisation, and network segmentation as the mechanism that keeps systems out of scope. Know the assessment ladder - merchant levels, self-assessment questionnaires versus a QSA-led Report on Compliance, and the Attestation of Compliance you will be asked to produce or consume. The FDE-relevant insight is that SAQ A (fully outsourced payment page) versus SAQ A-EP (your page controls the payment form) is a difference of one script tag, and that current PCI DSS requirements on payment-page script integrity and change detection make third-party tags on checkout a live issue. Your default engineering answer is always: do not let the PAN touch your systems.

resource.label: Stripe Docs - Integration security guide: validating PCI compliance, low-risk integrations and out-of-scope card data

subtopics.name: The LLM-specific compliance surface
subtopics.learn: This is where you add value no compliance lead can: articulate the AI-specific data flows. Cover training on customer data (API traffic is normally excluded by default - verify, do not assume), retention and abuse-monitoring windows and how zero-data-retention agreements change them, the model provider as a named subprocessor with notice obligations, and whether a BAA exists for healthcare traffic. Add the ones people miss: prompts and completions captured in your LLM observability tool are a second copy of regulated data in a second vendor; embeddings derived from personal data are still personal data; an LLM-as-judge or fallback model is a third processor nobody disclosed; and automated classification affecting individuals raises GDPR Art 22 and transparency obligations, plus EU AI Act duties depending on use. Write the AI data-flow paragraph for DefenderMate that you would hand a CISO.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform - Your data (retention, training, controls)

subtopics.name: Map once, answer many: crosswalks, questionnaires and machine-readable controls
subtopics.learn: Frameworks overlap by roughly 80 percent, so build one internal control set and crosswalk it outward rather than restarting per customer. Learn the shape of the standard questionnaires - CSA CAIQ against the Cloud Controls Matrix, and the SIG - and keep a maintained answer bank keyed to your control IDs so a 300-question review becomes an hour of review plus a short list of genuine gaps. Know that ISO 27001 is a certified management system while SOC 2 is an attestation report, and that a customer asking for both usually needs one. Look at OSCAL to understand where machine-readable control catalogues and system security plans are heading. Finish with the professional skill: writing a truthful 'not implemented, here is the compensating control and the date' row instead of a hopeful yes - one discovered overstatement costs more than ten honest gaps.

outcomes: You can produce a control map for DefenderMate with at least 30 rows, each carrying framework references, a named implementation mechanism, a retrievable evidence artifact, an owner and a test frequency, and a written justification for every 'not applicable'.

You can read a vendor SOC 2 Type II report and, in ten minutes, state the audit period, the criteria categories in scope, any exceptions, the carve-outs, and the complementary user entity controls that now belong to you.

You can draw DefenderMate's regulated data flow end to end - browser, webhook, Redis, Postgres, model provider, S3, CRM, email, logs and traces - and name every processor and subprocessor that touches personal data.

You can walk through a GDPR Art 17 erasure request store by store, including what happens in versioned S3, Kafka, the vector index, third-party logs and backups, and defend the backup answer without claiming something you cannot do.
You can answer a CAIQ or SIG questionnaire from your own answer bank, marking honest gaps with compensating controls and dates rather than aspirational yeses.
You can correctly use the terms controller, processor, business associate, BAA, CDE, PAN, Type I/Type II, addressable safeguard, DPIA and SCC in conversation without a compliance lead correcting you.
You can state, for any control you claim, exactly which command or API call produces the evidence, and run it in front of someone.
You can identify in a live conversation which questions you must route to legal, and say so without stalling the meeting.
failureModes: Regulated data leaks into telemetry: full request bodies, prompts and completions land in a third-party log or LLM-tracing SaaS that is not on the subprocessor list and has a 30-day retention nobody disclosed.
Erasure is implemented in Postgres only, and the deleted subject reappears from an S3 export, the analytics warehouse, HubSpot, or a restored backup that nobody re-processed.

The control map claims 'encrypted at rest' pointing at RDS storage encryption, and the auditor's follow-up - who can read the plaintext - reveals that every engineer with prod read access can, so the control fails on effectiveness.

Evidence is gathered as screenshots in the week before the audit, and the request for a complete population of production changes in the period cannot be satisfied because the emergency-change path bypassed the pipeline and left no record.
Sales commits to HIPAA before anyone checks whether a BAA exists with the model provider and the log vendor, and PHI has already been flowing through both for weeks.
A seeded staging or demo environment is loaded from a production dump, sits outside the audited boundary with weaker access controls, and is real customer data nobody counted.

The blocker turns out to be a complementary user entity control in the cloud provider's own SOC 2 - customer-side MFA, key configuration, access review - that was assumed to be inherited and was never implemented.
interviewQuestions: A hospital's compliance lead asks whether patient notes can be sent to a hosted LLM. What do you say in the meeting, what do you need to verify before you commit to anything, and what architecture would you propose if the answer turns out to be no?
Walk me through the difference between SOC 2 Type I and Type II, and give me a concrete reason a customer would reject a Type I report we just paid for.

Design the deletion path for a GDPR Article 17 request in a system with Postgres, Redis, versioned S3 exports, a vector index, Kafka and a third-party CRM. What can you not delete, and how do you defend that to the customer's DPO?

We discover that 20,000 records containing customer personal data have been written to application logs shipped to a third-party SaaS for the last nine months. Take me through the next 72 hours: what you do first, who decides what, and what you need from the system to answer their questions.
A prospect sends a 300-question security questionnaire and wants it back in three days. How do you run that, and how do you decide what to answer yes, no, and compensating control?

A customer says they will only buy if we deploy entirely inside their VPC so no data leaves their account. What does that actually change legally, what does it change operationally for us, and what breaks in the product?

Their payments team currently posts card numbers to their own backend before forwarding to a gateway. How do you reduce their PCI scope, and what do you have to be careful not to promise while doing it?
proofOfWork: Ship a public repository, compliance-pack, that turns the control map from theatre into running code for DefenderMate. It contains: (1) controls.yaml, one entry per control with framework crosswalk references (SOC 2 CC-series, GDPR articles, HIPAA 45 CFR 164 citations, PCI requirements), implementation, owner, frequency and status, rendered into the reviewable spreadsheet by a script; (2) an evidence/ collector - a make evidence target that hits the GitHub API for the merge population, dumps pg_policies and pg_roles, pulls the IAM credential report and AWS Config rule compliance, and writes dated JSON per control so evidence is generated, not screenshotted; (3) a data-flow diagram plus a one-page Art 30 record of processing and a subprocessor table listing every vendor that touches personal data, with region and retention; (4) a runnable erasure runbook, erase_subject.py, that deletes a test subject across Postgres, Redis, versioned S3, the search index and the CRM sandbox, and emits a signed proof-of-deletion report naming what was deleted, what was crypto-shredded and what remains in backups until the retention window expires; and (5) a two-page customer-facing security overview written in the register a CISO reads, ending with an honest gaps table carrying owners and dates. The test of the artifact is that a compliance lead can pick any row and you can produce its evidence live in under a minute.
